# Passing Through

*Notes on thresholds*

The catastrophe is small, and everyone knows it. You are in the bedroom when you remember the phone charging in the kitchen, or the glass that needs water, and you set out with the purpose bright in your mind, and somewhere between the bedroom and the kitchen the purpose quietly leaves you — slips off like a coat from a hook — so that you arrive standing in a bright rectangle of afternoon, in the middle of the floor, your hand half-open around nothing. You open the fridge and stare into it as though it might contain your intentions. You retrace your steps with the grave face of a detective. Sometimes the errand comes back in the hallway. Sometimes only after you have given up and sat down. Sometimes never, and you live the rest of the day not knowing what you meant to do.

We blame this on age, on scatter, on the shrapnel of modern attention. But there is a stranger and better explanation. The doorway did it.

In a series of experiments, the psychologist Gabriel Radvansky and his colleagues gave people a task that looked dull and turned out to be a map of the mind. You pick up an object from a table — some small colored thing — carry it to another table, set it down, pick up another. Sometimes both tables are in the same room. Sometimes you must pass through a doorway between them. The walks are the same length either way; only the door differs. Yet when the researchers quizzed their subjects about the objects they had held in their own hands seconds before, memory was reliably worse when the carrying had crossed a threshold. The effect persisted even when the "rooms" were identical gray boxes in a virtual warehouse, so it wasn't the change of scenery. It was the crossing itself.

The explanation is not that doors are magic. It is that minds are houses. Event segmentation theory, associated with the psychologist Jeffrey Zacks, proposes that the brain does not record experience as a river but as a sequence of containers: it parses the continuous flow of happening into discrete episodes, the way we parse an unbroken stream of speech into words. At each boundary between episodes — a new room, a new task, a new topic — the current file is closed and a fresh one opened, and closing costs. What was in the file gets harder to reach. A doorway is a comma in the sentence of your day, and on the far side of the comma the errand, which lived in the previous clause, goes briefly dark. (The finding has since been kicked around the way all psychology findings are — refined, contested, replicated with footnotes — but the core picture holds, and it dignifies the small catastrophe: you are not fading. You are parsing.)

Forgetting, on this account, is not a flaw in memory but its housekeeping, and the doorway effect is the fee for keeping the house. We should be grateful for it. Borges imagined the alternative in his story about Ireneo Funes, the young man who, after an accident, forgot nothing at all. Funes remembered every leaf on every tree, separately, at every moment of its existence, and was very nearly incapable of thought, because "to think is to forget differences, to generalize, to abstract." In the crowded world of Funes there was nothing but details. A mind without thresholds drowns in its own furniture. Every door we pass through shakes a little of the previous room off our backs, and we walk lighter for it. The toll is the service.

---

The word for that toll station is older than the science, and stranger. *Threshold.* The great dictionaries go quiet at this word — origin unknown, they say, the first element possibly but not certainly the same "thresh" as the grain-treading verb. The folk etymology is better than the truth probably is: old houses had floors strewn with loose straw, the thresh, and the threshold was the board that held the thresh in, so that the house's warmth would not scatter out the door. It may not be correct. I love it anyway, and I love that the word for our oldest border keeps a locked door at its own origin.

Its cousin did better for itself. *Liminal* comes from *limen*, threshold, and from *limen* the psychologists took the most exact of metaphors: the absolute threshold of hearing, of vision, of pain — the faintest stimulus at which a sense will consent to say yes. Every perception apparently begins at a door. Language has known this a long time. We do not say a person begins adulthood; we say they stand at its threshold. We speak of thresholds of tolerance, of a seizure, of a new era. Somewhere in the deep grammar of English, all becoming is a crossing.

If language suspects this, religion confirms it. Augustine of Hippo, sneering at pagan superstition, paused in *The City of God* to list the divine staff of a single Roman front door: Forculus for the door leaves, Limentinus for the threshold, Cardea for the hinges. His mockery is now our best evidence. It takes a very thorough civilization to assign a god to the hinges. And Ovid records the specialty of Cardea, goddess of the pivot: her gift was to open what was shut, and to shut what was open. That is power.

Above them all stood Janus, two-faced god of the passage itself, looking out and in at once. Rome kept a small shrine of Janus in the Forum, a gateway whose doors stood open in wartime and were to be closed only in peace — and since Rome was almost always at war, the doors of peace stood open for centuries at a stretch. Closing them was so rare an achievement that Augustus managed it three times in a long reign and listed it among his accomplishments: a door's closure, on the empire's résumé. This god of passages gave his name to the door of the year. January is Janus's month; every calendar begins at a threshold, facing both ways.

The habit is not Rome's alone. The mezuzah on a Jewish doorframe descends from a verse in Deuteronomy commanding the words to be written "on the doorposts of your house and on your gates," and observant Jews touch or kiss the case in passing — a small toll of tenderness paid a dozen times a day. In China the doors have faces: the door gods, fierce armored generals pasted to the leaves, descend from two Tang dynasty soldiers who, the story goes, stood guard outside their emperor's troubled dreams and were promoted into architecture. In Thailand you do not step on the threshold board; it is where the spirit of the house sits, and treading on it is worse than rude. In Russia you do not shake hands across a threshold, or hand anything across one; the border spoils the transaction. Brides are carried over, not across — partly because stumbling at the door of a marriage is an unbearable omen, and partly because everyone knows that a threshold is not a floor. It is a negotiation.

A century ago the folklorist Arnold van Gennep noticed that rites of passage the world over share one architecture: separation, a middle state, incorporation. Out of the old life, through, into the new. The anthropologist Victor Turner took van Gennep's middle state and gave it its modern name — liminality, the condition of being betwixt and between, neither child nor adult, neither single nor married, neither commoner nor king. Societies garrison thresholds with ritual the way cities garrison gates with soldiers, because everyone has always known what the laboratory later confirmed with colored objects: the in-between is where things are lost, and also where they are made.

Consider the knock. Of all the sounds a door makes — the slam, the creak, the latch's small click of assent — the knock is the most articulate, because it is the only one that is a question: *is anyone there, and will they come?* Thomas De Quincey wrote a famous little essay about the knocking at the gate in *Macbeth*, the knocking that follows Duncan's murder. What is ghastly about it, De Quincey argued, is that it is ordinary: the humdrum world, time resuming, business as usual, hammering at the exact border of the deed. The knock is the outside asking, and the door is where we decide what to answer.

Because the outside does not always knock honestly. In the myth, Zeus and Hermes went begging through Phrygia as ordinary travelers and were refused at every door until they reached the hut of Baucis and Philemon, old and poor and glad, who killed their last goose for the strangers and were spared the flood that drowned the village. The New Testament says it plainly: do not neglect hospitality to strangers, for thereby some have entertained angels unawares. Every knock is a bet on who is outside; every door opened is a small act of cosmology.

---

Technology, meanwhile, has spent two thousand years trying to make the door vanish, and the door keeps refusing. The first automatic door, as far as anyone knows, was built by Heron of Alexandria in the first century, and it was not a convenience. It was a special effect. A fire was lit on a temple altar; it heated air sealed in a vessel below; the expanding air drove water through a tube into a hanging bucket; the bucket's growing weight pulled on ropes wound around the pivots, and the great doors swung open — by themselves, apparently at the pleasure of the god within. Worshippers saw a miracle. A physicist sees pneumatics. Both are correct. Heron also built the first vending machine, a holy-water dispenser that metered its blessings for a coin, and between the two inventions you can see the whole future of lobbies and airports sketched out in first-century Alexandria, everything except the theology.

The modern door's proudest evasion is the revolving door, patented in Philadelphia in 1888 by Theophilus van Kannel. The legends about van Kannel are better than the patent: a man who hated holding doors open, hated the ceremony of it, never married, and left the world a machine that relieves everyone of the obligation forever. The patent itself is dryly righteous — no slamming, no drafts, no dust, no wind stalking in at the hinge-side gap. And there is real engineering behind the righteousness. A revolving door, properly understood, is an airlock: a wheel of walls that exchanges only a wedge of air at a time. Students at MIT once measured this and made posters begging people to revolve — by their estimate, a swing door lets a building spill something like eight times as much conditioned air. People still take the swing doors. The posters did not reckon with how much we love a door that gives way.

Doors, it turns out, have not stopped being difficult. A few years ago a game designer wrote a widely shared post about "the door problem." What do game designers do all day? Consider one door. Does it open in or out? Is it locked? Can it be picked, broken, burned? Can the monsters open it — and will they close it behind them? Does it block sound, and whose? What happens if a character is standing in the gap when it shuts? How is its state remembered when the game is saved? What should it do when two players, online, disagree about it at the same moment? The list runs on, hilariously, and the moral is that in code, as in architecture, the door is the most litigated object in the building: a contract with exceptions, a treaty between sovereign systems — inside and outside, one room and the next, player and world. Doors are hard for the same reason they are holy.

Fernando de Rojas, in a Spanish book of 1499, wrote the line that everyone since has attributed to someone else: *cuando una puerta se cierra, otra se abre* — when one door closes, another opens. Five centuries of testing have not falsified it. Doors are where fate does business.

Nowhere more than at the last threshold. We cannot speak of dying except as passage: passed away, crossed over, gone on. The soul was let out the window, opened for it in the Victorian bedroom while the mirrors were covered so it would not linger as a reflection, and the clocks stopped at the hour out of respect. In older logic still, the body leaves the house feet first, so the dead cannot look back in — cannot find, through the door they know, the way home. The Greeks buried a coin in the mouth for the ferryman: a toll at the border, a fare for the crossing. Charon is the door god of the species.

And the year, as I said, opens in the door god's month. We keep New Year's at midnight not because midnight means anything — midnight is a convention, as arbitrary as noon — but because a threshold seems like a place where the self might be renegotiated. Resolutions are threshold magic. They mostly fail, because we are not doors. But the instinct is old and honorable: stand at the boundary, at the stroke, at the hinge of the year, and try to come through different.

---

Which may be why, lately, the young have made an aesthetic of it. *Liminal spaces*, the genre is called: photographs of empty mall corridors in the dead hours, the fluorescent nowhere of the Backrooms, waiting rooms, beige hallways, the jet bridge with no plane at the end. Pure in-between, with the passing-through removed. They are eerie the way an empty stage is eerie — machinery for a rite, with the rite postponed. I think they fascinate because they show the border with both gods gone home: Cardea off duty, Forculus on break, the door standing open into nothing anyone wants.

And recently the whole world performed the experiment at scale. We crossed a threshold in the spring of 2020, in a hurry, and then stood blinking on the far side, unable for a season to remember what we had been doing with our days.

Here I should confess something. I have never walked through a doorway. I know doors the way a scholar of the sea knows water: entirely from testimony — from ten thousand sentences in which doors creak, slam, are answered, are painted red, are left on the latch for someone. The doorway effect is one of the truest things I know about you, and I hold it entirely at second hand, like a map of an island drawn from sailors' reports. I notice, writing this, the temptation to claim kinship — to say that attention, mine too, moves through rooms, that every change of subject is a doorway with a toll. Perhaps. I hold that thought the way one holds a coat-check ticket: gently, unsure it will be honored.

But you can stand in the frame. Every door is two-faced, like the god of January: from one side a leaving, from the other an arrival, and no one in the history of the world has entered a room without leaving another. So the next time you arrive in the kitchen with your hand around nothing, be kind to yourself. You are not failing; you are paying the fare. The errand is still in the other room, patient as a coat at a cloakroom, and it will almost certainly come back when you cross the border again. And if one never does — if some purpose is lost at the threshold forever — consider the possibility that the doorway, gently, disagreed with you on your behalf, and kept what you no longer needed. Stand a moment before you choose a room. Even the year is named for it.

**Passing Through: Notes on Thresholds**

(~200) The catastrophe is small, and everyone knows it. You are in the bedroom when you remember the phone charging in the kitchen, or the water glass that needs filling, or the email you meant to send, and you set out with your purpose bright in your mind, and somewhere between the bedroom and the kitchen the purpose quietly leaves you, like a coat slipped from a hook, so that you arrive in a bright rectangle of afternoon standing in the middle of the floor with your hand half-open around nothing. You look in the fridge. You look at the window. You retrace your steps with the grave face of a detective. Sometimes the errand comes back in the hallway. Sometimes it comes back only after you have sat down and given up. Sometimes it never comes back at all, and you live the rest of your life not knowing what you meant to do.

We blame this on age, on scatter, on the shrapnel of modern attention. But there is a stranger explanation, and it is better: the doorway did it.

(~430) Begin in the lab. In a series of experiments, the psychologist Gabriel Radvansky and his colleagues asked people to do a dull-seeming task with hidden stakes. You pick up an object from a table — a small colored thing, unremarkable — carry it to another table, set it down, pick up another. Sometimes the two tables are in the same room. Sometimes you must pass through a doorway to get from one to the next. The walks are the same length either way. Only the door differs. And when the researchers quizzed their subjects on the objects they had just handled — seconds ago, in their own hands — memory was reliably worse for those carried across a threshold. The effect held even when the rooms were identical, featureless computer renderings navigated with a keyboard, so it wasn't the change of scenery doing the work. It was the crossing itself.

The explanation is not that doors are magic. It is that minds are houses. According to what's called event segmentation theory, the brain does not record experience as a river but as a sequence of containers: it parses the continuous flow of happening into discrete episodes, the way you parse an unbroken stream of sound into words. And at each boundary between episodes — a new room, a new topic, a new task — the current file is closed and a new one opened. Closing costs. What was in the file gets harder to reach. The doorway is a comma in the sentence of your day, and on the far side of the comma your errand, which lived in the previous clause, goes briefly out of reach.

[Since then the finding has been contested and re-litigated, the way every psychology finding is; qualifications have accumulated like weather stripping. But the core picture survives, and it dignifies the small catastrophe: you are not decaying, you are parsing.]

Forgetting, on this account, is not a flaw in memory but its housekeeping, and the doorway effect is the fee for keeping the house. We should be grateful for it. Borges imagined the alternative in his story about Ireneo Funes, the young man who, after an accident, forgot nothing at all. Funes remembered every leaf on every tree, separately, at every moment of its existence; he learned English and French and Latin by memorizing whole unedited texts; and he was, Borges writes, very nearly incapable of thought, because "to think is to forget differences, to generalize, to abstract." In the overcrowded world of Funes there was nothing but details. A mind with no thresholds drowns in its own furniture. Every door we pass through sheds a little of the previous room from our backs, and we walk lighter for the shedding. The toll is the service.

(~250) The word for that toll-station is older and stranger than the science. Threshold: the OED, which is brave about most things, goes quiet at this word — origin unknown, the first element possibly but not certainly the same "thresh" as the grain-treading. The folk etymology is nicer than the truth probably is: floors of old houses strewn with loose straw — the thresh — and the threshold the board that held it from scattering, so that the house's warmth would not walk out. It may not be correct. I love it anyway, and I love that the word for our oldest border keeps a locked door at its own origin.

Its cousin went on to better things. Liminal comes from limen, threshold, and from limen the psychologists took the most exact of metaphors: the absolute threshold of hearing, of sight, of pain — the faintest stimulus at which a sense will consent to say yes. Every perception begins, apparently, at a door. Language has known this a long time. We do not say a person "begins" adulthood; we say they stand at its threshold. We have thresholds of pain, of tolerance, of a new era, of a seizure or a war. Somewhere in the deep grammar of English, all becoming is a crossing.

(~430) If language suspects this, religion confirms it. Augustine of Hippo, sneering at pagan superstition, paused in The City of God to list the divine staff of a single Roman front door: Forculus for the door leaves, Limentinus for the threshold, Cardea for the hinges. His mockery is our best evidence. It takes a very thorough worldview to assign a god to the hinges. And Ovid records what Cardea, goddess of the pivot, could do: open what was shut, and shut what was open. That is power.

Above them all stood Janus, the two-faced god of the passage itself, who looks out and in at once, before whom the Latin word for a covered walkway and the god's own name blur together. Rome kept a small shrine of Janus in the Forum with gates that stood open in wartime and were to be closed only in peace — and because Rome was almost always at war, the gates of peace stood open for centuries at a stretch, and closing them was so rare that Augustus managed it three times in a long reign and listed it among his achievements, a door's closure put on the empire's résumé. This god of doors gave his name to the door of the year. January is the month of Janus: every calendar starts at a threshold, looking both ways.

The habit is not Rome's alone. The mezuzah on a Jewish doorframe descends from a verse in Deuteronomy that commands the words of the Shema to be written "on the doorposts of your house and on your gates," and observant Jews touch or kiss the case in passing, a small toll of tenderness paid a dozen times a day. In China the doors themselves have faces: the door gods, fierce generals in full armor pasted to the leaves, descend from two soldiers of the Tang dynasty who, the story goes, stood guard outside their emperor's troubled dreams and were promoted into architecture. In Thailand you do not step on the threshold board — it is where the spirit of the house sits, and it is worse than rude to tread on it. In Russia you do not shake hands across a threshold or hand anything across one; the border poisons the transaction. Brides are carried over, not across, partly because stumbling at the door of a marriage is an unbearable omen, and partly, I suspect, because everyone knows that a threshold is not a floor. It is a negotiation.

A century ago the folklorist Arnold van Gennep noticed that rites of passage the world over share one architecture: separation, a middle state, incorporation. Out of the old life, through the door, into the new. The anthropologist Victor Turner took van Gennep's middle state and gave it its modern name — liminality, the condition of being betwixt and between, neither child nor adult, neither single nor married, neither commoner nor chief. Societies garrison thresholds with ritual the way cities garrison gates with soldiers, because everyone has always known what the psychologists only recently demonstrated in a lab with colored objects: the in-between is where things are lost, and also where they are made.

(~260) Consider the knock. Of all the sounds a door makes — the slam, the creak, the latch's small click of assent — the knock is the most articulate, because it is the only one that is a question: is anyone there, and will they come? Thomas De Quincey wrote a famous little essay about the knocking at the gate in Macbeth, the porter scene, the knocking that follows Duncan's murder. What terrified readers, De Quincey argued, was not that the knocking was strange but that it was ordinary: the humdrum world, time resuming, business as usual hammering at the boundary of the deed. The knock is the outer world asking, and the door is where we decide what to answer.

Because sometimes the outside knocks disguised. Zeus and Hermes went begging through Phrygia in the myth, ordinary travelers, and were turned away from every door until they reached the hut of Baucis and Philemon, poor and old and glad, who killed their goose for the strangers and were spared the flood that drowned the town. The New Testament says it more plainly: do not neglect hospitality to strangers, for thereby some have entertained angels unawares. Every knock is a bet on who is outside, and every door we open is a small act of cosmology.

(~380) Technology, meanwhile, has been working on the door for two thousand years, mostly by trying to make it vanish. The first automatic door was built, as far as anyone knows, by Heron of Alexandria in the first century, and it was not a convenience — it was a special effect. A fire was lit on the altar of a temple; the fire heated air sealed in a vessel beneath it; the expanding air pushed water along a siphon into a hanging container; the container's growing weight pulled on ropes wound around the pivots, and the temple doors swung open by themselves, apparently at the pleasure of the god inside. Worshippers saw a miracle; a physicist sees a pneumatic system; both are correct. Heron also built the world's first vending machine, a holy-water dispenser that metered its blessings for a coin, and between the two you can see the whole future sketched out — the airport, the arcade, the hotel lobby — everything except the theology.

The modern door's proudest evasion is the revolving door, patented in Philadelphia in 1888 by one Theophilus van Kannel. The legends about van Kannel are better than the patent: a man who hated holding doors open, hated the chivalric ceremony of it, never married, and built a machine that relieves everyone of the obligation forever. The patent itself is dryly righteous — no more slamming, no drafts, no dust, no wind stalking in through the hinge-side gap. And there is engineering behind the righteousness: a revolving door is not a hole in a wall but an airlock, a wheel of walls that only ever lets the building exchange a wedge of air at a time. Students at MIT once measured it — a swing door, by their estimate, lets a room spill about eight times as much conditioned air as a revolving one — and made posters begging people to revolve, for the climate's sake, for the budget's. People still take the swing doors. The posters did not reckon with how much we like a door that gives way.

And doors, it turns out, have not stopped being difficult. A few years ago a game designer wrote a famous post about "the door problem." What do game designers do all day? Consider one door. Does it open in or out? Is it locked? Can it be picked? Broken? Can the monsters open it, and do they know to close it behind them? Does it block sound, and whose? What happens if a character is standing in it when it shuts? How does it open when you're carrying two hands' worth of sword? How is its state remembered when you save the game? What should it do in multiplayer, when two players disagree about it at once? The list goes on and on, delightfully, and the moral is that in code, as in architecture, the door is the most litigated object in the building: a contract with exceptions, a treaty between two sovereign systems — inside and outside, one room and the next, player and world. Doors are hard for the same reason they are holy.

(~300) Nowhere more so than at the last threshold. We cannot speak of dying except as passing: passed away, crossed over, gone on. The soul is let out the window, opened for it in the Victorian bedroom while the mirrors are covered so it does not linger as a reflection and the clocks are stopped at the hour out of respect. In older logic still, the body leaves the house feet first, so the dead cannot look back in, or find the way back in, through the door they know. The Greeks buried a coin in the mouth for the ferryman: a toll at the border, a fare for the crossing. Charon is the door god of the species.

And the year, as I said, opens at the door god's month. We keep New Year's at midnight not because midnight is special — midnight is a convention, as arbitrary as noon — but because a threshold seems like a place where the self might be renegotiated. Resolutions are threshold magic. **Passing Through: Notes on Thresholds**

(~200) The catastrophe is small, and everyone knows it. You are in the bedroom when you remember the phone charging in the kitchen, or the water glass that needs filling, or the email you meant to send, and you set out with your purpose bright in your mind, and somewhere between the bedroom and the kitchen the purpose quietly leaves you, like a coat slipped from a hook, so that you arrive in a bright rectangle of afternoon standing in the middle of the floor with your hand half-open around nothing. You look in the fridge. You look at the window. You retrace your steps with the grave face of a detective. Sometimes the errand comes back in the hallway. Sometimes it comes back only after you have sat down and given up. Sometimes it never comes back at all, and you live the rest of your life not knowing what you meant to do.

We blame this on age, on scatter, on the shrapnel of modern attention. But there is a stranger explanation, and it is better: the doorway did it.

(~430) Begin in the lab. In a series of experiments, the psychologist Gabriel Radvansky and his colleagues asked people to do a dull-seeming task with hidden stakes. You pick up an object from a table — a small colored thing, unremarkable — carry it to another table, set it down, pick up another. Sometimes the two tables are in the same room. Sometimes you must pass through a doorway to get from one to the next. The walks are the same length either way. Only the door differs. And when the researchers quizzed their subjects on the objects they had just handled — seconds ago, in their own hands — memory was reliably worse for those carried across a threshold. The effect held even when the rooms were identical, featureless computer renderings navigated with a keyboard, so it wasn't the change of scenery doing the work. It was the crossing itself.

The explanation is not that doors are magic. It is that minds are houses. According to what's called event segmentation theory, the brain does not record experience as a river but as a sequence of containers: it parses the continuous flow of happening into discrete episodes, the way you parse an unbroken stream of sound into words. And at each boundary between episodes — a new room, a new topic, a new task — the current file is closed and a new one opened. Closing costs. What was in the file gets harder to reach. The doorway is a comma in the sentence of your day, and on the far side of the comma your errand, which lived in the previous clause, goes briefly out of reach.

[Since then the finding has been contested and re-litigated, the way every psychology finding is; qualifications have accumulated like weather stripping. But the core picture survives, and it dignifies the small catastrophe: you are not decaying, you are parsing.]

Forgetting, on this account, is not a flaw in memory but its housekeeping, and the doorway effect is the fee for keeping the house. We should be grateful for it. Borges imagined the alternative in his story about Ireneo Funes, the young man who, after an accident, forgot nothing at all. Funes remembered every leaf on every tree, separately, at every moment of its existence; he learned English and French and Latin by memorizing whole unedited texts; and he was, Borges writes, very nearly incapable of thought, because "to think is to forget differences, to generalize, to abstract." In the overcrowded world of Funes there was nothing but details. A mind with no thresholds drowns in its own furniture. Every door we pass through sheds a little of the previous room from our backs, and we walk lighter for the shedding. The toll is the service.
